title: Throughput tuning deep dive - BrightScale / Redwood
summary: Technical deep dive focused on throughput tuning for BrightScale's inference workloads. Covered continuous batching behavior, scheduler parameters (max_num_seqs, max_batch_tokens), token limits and tail latency, KV cache warmup/affinity, and tradeoffs for quantization profiles on A100 vs T4. Agreed next steps: Redwood to run a tailored benchmark with suggested knobs and share a tuning guide; BrightScale to provide a sample traffic profile and a small model artifact for tests.
next_steps: Redwood (Luis): run 4 benchmark runs with max_num_seqs=4/8 and report p50/p90/p99 by 2026-07-22
BrightScale (Danielle): share 48h sample traffic and model artifact ( ~1.3B encoder-decoder ) by 2026-07-19
Schedule follow-up benchmark review with AE/SE/Customer in week of 2026-07-27
action_items: Luis Ortega: prepare tuning runs (A100x2, A100x4) with continuous batching and the three scheduler knob sets - due 2026-07-22
Danielle Park: export anonymized traffic (48h) and upload to shared s3 link - due 2026-07-19
Maya Chen: share Redwood throughput tuning doc and quantization guidance - due 2026-07-17
transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-07-15 16:00 UTC
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Danielle Park (BrightScale Head of ML Infra), Omar Farouk (BrightScale SRE), Priya Iyer (BrightScale ML Engineer)

[00:00] Maya Chen: hi everyone, thanks for joining, we thought we'd use this time to dig into throughput tuning for your production workloads, specifically continuous batching and scheduler knobs
[00:12] Danielle Park: yep thanks, we're seeing good quality but cost is through the roof and p99 spikes during our peak window.
[00:20] Luis Ortega: ok quick question, what's your current infra, GPUs and networking?
[00:25] Omar Farouk: we're on k8s in GCP, mix of A100 80GB and some T4s for cheap spots. we route traffic through a vpc connector — sorry, through the private vpc.
[00:37] Priya Iyer: model is a 1.3B encoder-decoder variant, 2k token context max in theory but typical requests are 120 tokens.
[00:47] Luis Ortega: good, that distribution matters a lot. continuous batching in Redwood tries to balance latency SLO vs throughput by batching similar seq lengths together and using max_num_seqs as the upper bound for concurrent sequences in a batch.
[01:00] Danielle Park: can you unpack max_num_seqs? we tried raising it and saw reduced cost but tail latency shot up.
[01:08] Luis Ortega: sure, max_num_seqs controls how many concurrent request sequences the scheduler will allow to combine in the same generation batch. higher values increase GPU utilization but can increase head-of-line blocking when one long sequence has to wait for shorter ones to finish decoding tokens.
[01:22] Maya Chen: important point: token limits and the max_batch_tokens parameter work together. if you have a lot of short requests, you want a higher max_num_seqs but cap total batch tokens so a single long sequence doesn't blow latency.
[01:33] Omar Farouk: when we raised max_num_seqs from 4 to 12 the avg latency dropped but p99 jumped from 420ms to 1.8s, which users notice.
[01:45] Luis Ortega: that's classic. one knob we use: hierarchical batching --- prefer grouping by length buckets then combine buckets up to token limit. you can tune bucket size and wait-time thresholds (like 8ms vs 30ms).
[01:58] Priya Iyer: does Redwood do KV cache affinity across requests? our workloads have a lot of repeated prefixes.
[02:04] Luis Ortega: yes we have prefix/KV caching, but affinity depends on routing. in Dedicated and Private modes you can enable session affinity on the router so the cached KV stays warm on the same replica. On hosted mode it's probabilistic unless you pin sessions.
[02:19] Danielle Park: pinning sessions kills our ability to autoscale though.
[02:24] Maya Chen: correct, it's a tradeoff. for hot prefixes we recommend a small pool of pinned replicas to hold cache and a larger elastic pool for cold traffic.
[02:34] Omar Farouk: curious about quantization — we've tried int8 and saw some hallucination increase. what's Redwood's view?
[02:41] Luis Ortega: quantization can change model distribution slightly; we recommend running quality evals on representative prompts. there are mid-quantization profiles (like q4_0 vs q4_k) that balance perf vs quality. for certain encoder-decoder models q4_k tends to preserve quality better at cost of a bit slower decode.
[02:58] Priya Iyer: any hardware differences? we have mixed A100 and T4.
[03:02] Luis Ortega: yes A100 with more memory helps larger batch tokens and KV cache residency, T4s are cheaper but you may need lower max_num_seqs and smaller batch token caps. Also CUDA kernel selection differs, some optimizations only hit on newer drivers.
[03:18] Danielle Park: can you walk through scheduler knob set examples? like conservative, balanced, aggressive?
[03:24] Luis Ortega: sure. conservative: max_num_seqs=2, max_batch_tokens=2048, bucket_wait_ms=8, prefer latency. balanced: max_num_seqs=4-8, max_batch_tokens=4096, bucket_wait_ms=15. aggressive: max_num_seqs=12-16, max_batch_tokens=8192, bucket_wait_ms=30 — aggressive gives best throughput but watch tail latency.
[03:50] Omar Farouk: how do we measure impact without affecting prod? can we run shadow traffic?
[03:55] Maya Chen: yes Redwood supports shadowing or A/B routes. you can replay sampled traffic into a dedicated test pool with identical HW. Luis, we did a replay for them last week?
[04:06] Luis Ortega: yup we replay 1 hour windows and generate p50/p90/p99 and cost delta. that convinced one customer to go balanced.
[04:14] Priya Iyer: about KV cache warmup, what are the best practices?
[04:19] Luis Ortega: pre-warming by replaying hot prefixes is effective. also keep a tiny instance of pinned replicas for very hot traffic. TTL on KV entries should match the expected session length; if you set it too long you waste memory, too short and you miss gains.
[04:33] Danielle Park: does Redwood expose cache hit rates per model/route?
[04:36] Maya Chen: yes Console shows token-level cache hit %, per-route. that was one feature BrightScale wanted, right?
[04:42] Danielle Park: yes that's huge.
[04:44] [05:00] Luis Ortega: (walking through a slide) here's a typical tuning exercise: 1) profile request length distribution 2) set initial scheduler knobs (balanced) 3) run replayed traffic across three knob sets 4) inspect p50/p90/p99 and cost per 1M tokens 5) iterate on bucketing thresholds or session affinity
[05:25] Omar Farouk: about token limits: we cap at 2k in our client. should we reduce that?
[05:30] Luis Ortega: if long tails are rare, reducing max_input_tokens to 1024 at the API layer prevents long requests from holding batches; for users needing long context you can offer a dedicated long-context route with lower max_num_seqs or dedicated hardware.
[05:46] Priya Iyer: our biggest pain is periodic p99 spikes during human-in-the-loop sessions — long completions every few minutes.
[05:54] Luis Ortega: consider isolating interactive sessions to a low-concurrency, low-latency pool (conservative knobs) and run background batch scoring on aggressive pools. Smart routing can do this by route label or API key.
[06:12] Danielle Park: can Redwood do automatic knob tuning? like adaptive scheduler?
[06:18] Luis Ortega: we have adaptive policies that adjust bucket_wait_ms and max_num_seqs based on observed latency vs SLO, but it's heuristic and needs a warm baseline. we can enable adaptive on a test pool.
[06:30] Maya Chen: note that adaptive policies can oscillate if your traffic has very spiky bursts; you want smoothing windows.
[06:38] [07:00] Priya Iyer: question on measuring p99 for GPU decode variability — noise from CUDA scheduling sometimes causes variance, how do you filter that out?
[07:10] Luis Ortega: we run multiple repeats and report trimmed means and percentiles, and separate out kernel preemption events. also check host-level noise — CPU throttling or noisy neighbors on multi-tenant nodes can add jitter.
[07:25] Omar Farouk: any advice on k8s node sizing? pod-level CPU/IO settings?
[07:30] Luis Ortega: make sure your node has enough CPU for the runtime threads that handle batching and kernel dispatch; we recommend pinning a CPU quota per GPU of ~8-12 vCPU for high throughput. watch NVMe bandwidth for model KV spills.
[07:50] Danielle Park: we saw a crash when batch tokens spiked; logs show OOM on the decoder.
[07:56] Luis Ortega: that could be unbounded batching in config or a mis-configured max_batch_tokens. Also check per-process max mem and CUDA mem fragmentation. We can help run leak checks.
[08:10] Maya Chen: quick pause — any regulatory constraints? BrightScale: do you need data residency or special logging for on-prem?
[08:18] Danielle Park: not for this use-case, but we will want to run Private for some customers in EU later. question: will these knobs differ on Private deployments?
[08:26] Luis Ortega: same knobs apply; you just have more control over routing and session affinity. Private gives you direct network control for KV affinity so caching is usually more effective.
[08:34] Priya Iyer: can you show a sample result from a prior benchmark?
[08:38] Luis Ortega: sure (screen share) example: balanced knobs on A100x4 with mix traffic gave p50 180ms p90 320ms p99 520ms and cost baseline. aggressive got p50 120ms p90 240ms p99 1.2s but 40% lower cost.
[09:02] Omar Farouk: and on T4?
[09:05] Luis Ortega: same config on T4s p50 was 230ms p90 450ms p99 900ms and cost wins smaller; recommended lower concurrency.
[09:16] Danielle Park: that 1.2s p99 is scary. can we mitigate with circuit breakers?
[09:20] Maya Chen: yes set client-side timeouts and server side fallbacks: e.g., fall back to a smaller model or reply with partial tokens; Redwood supports model variant fallback.
[09:31] Priya Iyer: variant fallback sounds useful. is there an opt-in in the API?
[09:34] Luis Ortega: yes you can define fallback chains per route and a hard timeout perchain. fallback can reduce tail events but needs evaluation for quality.
[09:44] [10:00] Danielle Park: let's talk about experiments we should run immediately.
[10:04] Luis Ortega: run three replays: conservative, balanced, aggressive with the same 60-minute sampled window. capture p50/p90/p99, cost per 1M tokens, and cache hit %. Also try adding a pinned 2-replica cache pool to test warm hit improvements.
[10:20] Maya Chen: and Luis will share a configured JSON for the scheduler and a short script to run replays.
[10:27] Danielle Park: how long does a replay take?
[10:29] Luis Ortega: depends on window and speed, but for 60 minutes it usually runs in wallclock 10-20 minutes if scaled on dedicated test nodes.
[10:37] Omar Farouk: are there any non-obvious knobs we should watch? like response truncation, prefill sizes?
[10:43] Luis Ortega: prefill chunking and pre-tokenization size matter; small prefill chunks can increase scheduling overhead. Also watch internal batching timeouts and the interop between request arrival and decoder steps.
[10:58] Priya Iyer: what about backpressure to clients? how to throttle to prevent overload?
[11:02] Maya Chen: Redwood supports rate limits and token quotas per key, and route-level throttles. Also you can return standard Retry-After headers.
[11:10] Danielle Park: do you have an example config for mixed hardware?
[11:14] Luis Ortega: yes we can supply a multi-pool routing policy: route small/interactive to A100 low-latency pool, send bulk scoring to T4 aggressive pool. give you the JSON map.
[11:26] Priya Iyer: let's discuss quantization again — we want to test q4_k and q4_0 side-by-side on our prompt set.
[11:32] Luis Ortega: recommended approach: run forking evals on the same replay dataset and compare standard eval metrics plus human spot-checks on a small sample. we'll include quantization config in the repo.
[11:44] Omar Farouk: any other observability tips to identify causes of p99 spikes?
[11:49] Luis Ortega: instrument per-step timing, show kernel latency distributions, separate enqueue vs decode vs network. Redwood Console exposes these breakdowns.
[12:00] Danielle Park: okay good. for the benchmark runs — please include per-host CPU/mem metrics and nvlink stats if available.
[12:07] Luis Ortega: will do.
[12:09] Maya Chen: quick recap of agreed experiment matrix and owners?
[12:14] Danielle Park: I'll upload traffic and model.
[12:17] Luis Ortega: I'll run the three knob sets and the pinned cache experiment.
[12:21] Maya Chen: I'll share the tuning doc and coordinate follow-up.
[12:27] [12:40] Priya Iyer: thank you, this was really helpful.
[12:45] Maya Chen: thanks all, we'll follow up in email with links.

End transcript.
